name: Usman dan Fodio
info: Usman dan Fodio was a Fulani Islamic scholar and preacher born in Gobir in 1754, who led a religious and social movement against the Hausa rulers and founded the Sokoto Caliphate, which he ruled as its first caliph until 1817.

facts.born: 15 December 1754 in Maratta, in Gobir; a Fulani of the Toronkawa clan, son of the scholar Muhammad Fodio and Hauwa bint Muhammad
facts.role: Islamic scholar, teacher and writer; Commander of the Faithful (Amīr al-Muʾminīn), named by his followers in 1804; founder and first caliph of the Sokoto Caliphate
facts.known: preaching tours in Gobir, Kebbi and Zamfara from 1774; the community at Degel; the hijra to Gudu and the jihad against Gobir; the founding of the Sokoto Caliphate; the education of women; more than a hundred books and many poems in Arabic, Fulfulde and Hausa

t: Born into a Fulani family of scholars in Gobir, Usman dan Fodio preached for years among the peasants and herders of Hausaland, criticising its rulers for taxation, enslavement and what he judged to be un-Islamic practices.

When the king of Gobir moved against his community, he and his followers withdrew to Gudu in 1804, named him Commander of the Faithful and fought a jihad that by 1808 had defeated the rulers of Gobir, Kano, Katsina and other Hausa kingdoms.

He handed the running of the new state to his son Muhammed Bello and his brother Abdullahi, and returned to teaching and writing; the Sokoto Caliphate outlasted him by almost a century, until the British conquest.
dyk: Usman dan Fodio held that women should receive the same education as men and put them in the same classrooms; several of his daughters became scholars and writers, and one of them, Nana Asmaʼu, translated some of his work into local languages.
ev: Usman is born in Maratta, in Gobir, into a Fulani family of the Toronkawa clan
He begins itinerant preaching, first in Gobir and Kebbi and later in Zamfara
A mystical vision leads him to believe he has the power to work miracles and to teach his own litany, or wird
Yunfa, the new king of Gobir and once Usman's student, revokes the autonomy of Degel and tries to have him killed
Usman and his followers leave Degel for Gudu and name him Commander of the Faithful; the jihad begins with the victory at Tabkin Kwotto
By this year Usman has defeated the rulers of Gobir, Kano, Katsina and other Hausa kingdoms
The caliphate's administration is reorganised, with Muhammed Bello and Abdullahi dan Fodio governing east and west
Usman dies in Sokoto and his son Muhammed Bello succeeds him as the second caliph

sections.early:
Usman dan Fodio was born on 15 December 1754 in Maratta, in Gobir. His name means “son of Fodiye”, his father, Muhammad Fodio, having earned the Fulani title Fodiye, “the learned”. The family were Toronkawa, descended from scholars who had moved into Hausaland from Futa Tooro in the 1300s; his father later moved them to Degel. His mother, Hauwa, came from a line of literary scholars, and she and his father were his first teachers. His grandmother Ruqayyah was a respected ascetic and teacher whose work was popular among scholars of the 18th and 19th centuries. Family tradition, repeated by Ahmadu Bello, holds that Hauwa descended from the Prophet Muhammad through Idris I of Morocco.

He studied the Quran with his father and then with other teachers, among them his relatives Uthman Bn Duri and Muhammad Sambo, and then Jibril bin Umar, a leading religious figure who supported jihad. Jibril later fell out with him over how a Muslim should be defined. At the age of 20 Usman set up a school in Degel, where he taught and preached. In 1786 he attended the assembly of his cousin Muhammad bn Raji and received further certification. By 1787 he was writing books in Arabic and long poems in Fulfulde.
sections.rise:
In 1774 Usman began preaching as an itinerant mallam. He preached for twelve years in Gobir and Kebbi and then for five years in Zamfara; his students included his younger brother Abdullahi and Yunfa, a future king of Gobir. He condemned the ruling elite for enslavement, idol worship, sacrificial rituals, overtaxation, arbitrary rule and greed, insisted on the Maliki school of law in worship, commerce and criminal law, and denounced pagan customs and inheritance practices that denied women their shares. His following grew among peasants and the lower classes, among slaves, and among Tuareg and Fulani herders whose cattle officials had seized.

He broke from the royal court and founded a religious community at Degel, where he stayed about twenty years. In 1789 a vision led him to teach his own litany, and in the 1790s he had visions of Abdul Qadir Gilani and was initiated into the Qadiriyya, of whose brotherhood he later became head. Around 1788–89 the ageing Sultan Bawa of Gobir summoned him to Magami and granted five concessions, among them freedom for prisoners and respect for those who wore the turban of his community. In 1797–98 Nafata, Bawa's successor, reversed this policy, banning preaching, turbans and veils, and conversions.
sections.deeds:
In 1802 Yunfa, who had succeeded Nafata, revoked Degel's autonomy and tried to have Usman killed at Alkalawa. When a Gobir force returning with Muslim prisoners passed Degel and was challenged, Yunfa's forces attacked Gimbana. Usman wrote that Muslims under persecution must emigrate, and in 1804 his community left for Gudu, a journey of four or five days; Muslims from across Hausaland joined them. His followers named him Commander of the Faithful, with Abdullahi first and Muhammed Bello second to give the salute of allegiance. At about fifty he was old and weak and took no part in the fighting.

The first major battle, Tabkin Kwotto in June 1804, was won by Abdullahi against the larger Gobir force. At Tsuntsua, two miles from the Gobir capital, the Muslims lost about 2,000 men, 200 of them Quran memorisers, according to Bello; they then took Kebbi and fought off a joint attack at Alwassa, where Bello recorded about a thousand dead. Usman appointed fourteen leaders to take the jihad to their own regions. By 1808 he had defeated the rulers of Gobir, Kano, Katsina and other Hausa kingdoms. In 1812 Bello and Abdullahi were given the western and eastern governance, and Usman returned to teaching and writing. Judges, market inspectors and prayer leaders were appointed, and an Islamic tax and land system was set up.
sections.opponents:
Usman's chief opponents were the Gobir kings Bawa, Nafata and Yunfa. Abdullahi dan Fodio's account, written at the Shehu's insistence, says the king of Gobir terrorised his followers, sold captured men, women and children into slavery before their eyes and ordered Usman to leave without his followers; it is the account of one side. The sultans of Hausaland were, in Usman's own words in Tanbih al-ikhwan, “undoubtedly unbelievers, even though they may profess the religion of Islam”. After Kwotto many Hausa kings and chiefs launched a strong assault on Muslim communities in their territories, and a commercial embargo was placed on Gudu.

Within the learned world he had other opponents. Jibril bin Umar disagreed with him over who counts as a Muslim, and Elkanemi of Borno objected to his education of women, to which Usman responded in writing. The motives of his allies were also questioned. According to Bello, the friendship of the Zamfara leaders came from their hostility to Gobir rather than from adherence to Islam, and the villagers were unwilling to sell the Muslims maize. Murray Last holds that the campaigns can be explained as a search for food, pasture and water for cattle.
sections.last:
After the reorganisation of 1812 Usman gave his time to teaching and writing about Islam and to building a government grounded in Islamic law. In 1815 he moved to Sokoto, where Bello built him a house in the western suburbs. He died there on 20 April 1817, at the age of 62. Gidado dan Laima listed two wives, his first cousin Maymuna, with whom he had 11 children including the twins Hasan and Nana Asmaʼu, and Aisha, known as Gaabdo and Iyya Garka, who was famed for her Islamic learning and outlived him by many decades.

His son Muhammed Bello succeeded him as Commander of the Faithful and became the second caliph of the Sokoto Caliphate, and Abdullahi was given the title Emir of Gwandu and charge of the western emirates. All the Hausa states, parts of Nupe and Fulani outposts in Bauchi and Adamawa were then ruled by one political and religious system. By 1830 the jihad had engulfed most of what is now northern Nigeria and northern Cameroon. From his time until the British conquest at the beginning of the 20th century there were twelve caliphs.
sections.legacy:
Under Usman the caliphate expanded into present-day Burkina Faso, Cameroon, southern Niger and most of northern Nigeria, and at the time it was the largest state south of the Sahara. It combined an Islamic state with a modified Hausa monarchy. David Westerlund described the result as a federal theocratic state, with extensive autonomy for emirates, which recognised the spiritual authority of the caliph. The nomadic Fulani herders were settled and mosques and schools were built; Arabic, Hausa and Fulfulde poetry revived, and Islam was taught in Hausa and Fulfulde.

Usman wrote more than a hundred books, on law, government, society and religion, and many poems; estimates of his poems range from 118 to about 480. His litanies are still widely practised. Many Muslims regard him as a mujaddid, a divinely sent renewer of the faith, and the Encyclopedia Britannica has treated him as the most important reforming leader of the 19th-century Western Sudan. His movement followed the jihads of Futa Bundu, Futa Tooro and Fouta Djallon, and inspired later ones, among them those of Seku Amadu, who founded the Massina Empire, and Omar Saidou Tall, founder of the Toucouleur Empire, who married one of his granddaughters.

summary: Usman dan Fodio (1754–1817), a Fulani scholar from Gobir, preached for years against the Hausa rulers, withdrew with his followers in 1804 and led a jihad that by 1808 had defeated Gobir, Kano and Katsina. He founded the Sokoto Caliphate, left its government to his son Muhammed Bello and his brother Abdullahi, and wrote more than a hundred books.
notes: The article contradicts itself on the founding date: the lede says the caliphate was founded in 1803, while the body places the hijra to Gudu and the first battles in 1804 (Hijra 'Thursday in the year 1218 (1804)', Tabkin Kwotto June 1804). 1804 used, 1803 left out.
Ihya al-sunna: one passage says it was finished 'by 1773', before the preaching began in 1774 and the school at age 20 (c. 1774); the date is left out.
Poems: the Notable works section says 118 poems, the Writings section about 480; both numbers stated in the text. Books: 'more than a hundred' and 'hundreds' both appear; 'more than a hundred' used.
Preaching: twelve years in Gobir and Kebbi then five in Zamfara from 1774 (17 years), but the Degel community 'for 20 years' and the 1789 vision; not reconciled.
Bawa's summons: dated 1788–89 in one place and described as 'ten years earlier' than Nafata's 1797–98 ban in another; 'around 1788–89' used. Bawa is called 75 years old and ailing.

Usman's age at the jihad is given as 50; 1804 minus 1754 is 50, consistent. The article says the title Commander of the Believers was given and also that the Abdullahi candidacy was proposed; only the naming is told.

Tsuntsua: the dead of about 2,000 are Bello's figure, also stated as the article's own narrative; the article places it in Ramadan after harvest of October 1804, which would be early 1805 by the calendar; the year is left out of the text.
Death: the article says 'at the age of 62' and gives the place as Sokoto; no cause given.

Left out: the Hausa translation of 'five concessions' details beyond two; the list of notable companions; the economic ideas (hisba, waqf, zakat, bayt al-mal) beyond the market inspectors; land reform; the 'In fiction' line.
The article says 'Usman declared jihad against the Hausa land and defeated them' in the lede; its body shows the war was begun after Gobir's attack. The profile follows the body.
Article text near the Kwotto section includes a gap (a poem by a Bornu scholar is introduced but not quoted); not used.
References: left empty for the editor.
